takeaways: In angle modulation the message moves the instantaneous phase; PM ties the phase to m(t), FM ties the frequency to m(t), so the FM phase holds the integral of m(t).
Narrowband FM has one sideband pair turned 90° to the carrier; wideband FM has many lines spaced f<sub>m</sub> apart, sized by J<sub>n</sub>(β), with the total power fixed at A<sub>c</sub>²/2.
Carson's rule 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>) is the bandwidth to allow: 180 kHz for mono broadcast FM and 256 kHz with the 53 kHz stereo baseband.

Direct FM pulls an LC oscillator with a varactor and needs AFC; Armstrong FM starts from a crystal with a tiny deviation and multiplies it, with a mixer between the multipliers to land on the channel.

Classic FM detectors turn frequency into amplitude or phase with tuned circuits, then use diodes; the Foster-Seeley gives an S-curve zero at f<sub>c</sub>, and the ratio detector trades half the output for built-in limiting.
With the noise measured in the message band, the figure of merit is 1/3 at best for AM, 1 for DSB-SC and SSB, and (3/2)β² for FM: FM buys output SNR with bandwidth.
FM keeps its advantage only above threshold, near a 10 dB carrier-to-noise ratio in the IF band; wider deviation needs a stronger carrier to reach it.
Pre-emphasis at the transmitter and de-emphasis at the receiver leave the programme flat and cut the treble noise, 13.2 dB for 75 µs and a 15 kHz band.
FM stereo keeps mono sets working by sending L + R at baseband, L − R on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier, and a 19 kHz pilot that the receiver doubles.

bank.q: Define instantaneous phase and instantaneous frequency of a sinusoid. Starting from v(t) = A cos[2πf<sub>c</sub> t + φ(t)], show that in PM the instantaneous frequency is f<sub>c</sub> + (k<sub>p</sub>/2π)·dm/dt, and explain why FM needs an integrator before a phase modulator.
outline: Write v(t) = A cos θ(t) and define θ(t) as the instantaneous phase in radians
Differentiate θ(t) to get f<sub>i</sub>(t) = (1/2π) dθ/dt
For PM, φ(t) = k<sub>p</sub> m(t), so f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> + (k<sub>p</sub>/2π) dm/dt
For FM, φ(t) = 2πk<sub>f</sub> ∫m dτ, so f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> + k<sub>f</sub> m(t)
PM follows the slope of the message, FM the message itself; a phase modulator gives FM only if fed with ∫m
answer: Instantaneous phase. Write the wave as v(t) = A cos θ(t). The whole angle θ(t), in radians, is the instantaneous phase. For an unmodulated carrier θ(t) = 2πf<sub>c</sub> t, a straight line of slope 2πf<sub>c</sub>.

Instantaneous frequency. Define f<sub>i</sub>(t) = (1/2π) dθ/dt in hertz: the slope of the phase, turned from rad/s to cycles per second. For the unmodulated carrier f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>, as it should be.

answer.text: Angle-modulated wave. With θ(t) = 2πf<sub>c</sub> t + φ(t):
answer.pre:
f<sub>i</sub>(t) = (1/2π) d/dt [2πf<sub>c</sub> t + φ(t)]
       = f<sub>c</sub> + (1/2π) dφ/dt

answer.text: PM. The phase sensitivity k<sub>p</sub> (rad/V) sets φ(t) = k<sub>p</sub> m(t). Then:

answer: So in PM the frequency deviation follows the slope of the message. For a tone m = A<sub>m</sub> cos 2πf<sub>m</sub> t the deviation is −k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> f<sub>m</sub> sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t, peak k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> f<sub>m</sub>: it grows with the tone frequency even at a fixed amplitude.

answer.text: FM. The frequency sensitivity k<sub>f</sub> (Hz/V) must make f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> + k<sub>f</sub> m(t). Working back, dφ/dt = 2πk<sub>f</sub> m(t), so:
answer.pre:
φ(t) = 2πk<sub>f</sub> ∫₀ᵗ m(τ) dτ
v(t) = A cos[2πf<sub>c</sub> t + 2πk<sub>f</sub> ∫₀ᵗ m(τ) dτ]

answer: Why the integrator. A phase modulator makes φ(t) = k<sub>p</sub> × (its input). If its input is ∫m(τ)dτ, then φ(t) = k<sub>p</sub> ∫m dτ, and f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> + (k<sub>p</sub>/2π) m(t): the frequency follows m(t), which is FM with k<sub>f</sub> = k<sub>p</sub>/2π. Without the integrator the same block gives PM. This is how the Armstrong transmitter makes FM from a crystal-driven phase modulator.

Units. k<sub>p</sub> is in rad/V and k<sub>f</sub> in Hz/V; the 2π in the FM phase turns cycles into radians, and it cancels against the 1/2π of the frequency definition, leaving f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> + k<sub>f</sub> m(t).

Numeric check. With k<sub>f</sub> = 3 kHz/V and A<sub>m</sub> = 2 V at 5 kHz, FM gives Δf = 6 kHz (β = 1.2); a phase modulator with k<sub>p</sub> = 0.8 rad/V gives Δθ = 1.6 rad and Δf = 1.6 × 5000 = 8 kHz, the values of the chapter's worked example.

bank.q: Explain the spectrum of a tone-modulated FM signal using Bessel functions. Distinguish narrowband and wideband FM, and state and justify Carson's rule.
outline: Write v(t) = A Σ J<sub>n</sub>(β) cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + n f<sub>m</sub>)t; lines at f<sub>c</sub> ± n f<sub>m</sub> with amplitude A|J<sub>n</sub>(β)|
Carrier amplitude A J<sub>0</sub>(β) can vanish (β = 2.405); total power A²/2 since Σ J<sub>n</sub>² = 1
NBFM: β small, only J<sub>0</sub> and J<sub>1</sub> matter, bandwidth 2f<sub>m</sub>, lower sideband negative
WBFM: many sidebands, bandwidth about 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>)
Carson: J<sub>n</sub> falls fast beyond n ≈ β + 1, so 2(β + 1)f<sub>m</sub> holds about 98 % or more of the power

answer.text: The wave. For a tone, s(t) = A cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t + β sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t), β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>. The factor exp(jβ sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t) is periodic in 1/f<sub>m</sub>, and its Fourier coefficients are the Bessel functions J<sub>n</sub>(β). So:
answer.pre:
s(t) = A Σ J<sub>n</sub>(β) cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + n f<sub>m</sub>)t,   n = −∞ … ∞
J<sub>−n</sub>(β) = (−1)ⁿ J<sub>n</sub>(β)

answer: Reading the spectrum. There is a line at f<sub>c</sub> (amplitude A J<sub>0</sub>(β)) and pairs at f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>c</sub> ± 2f<sub>m</sub> and so on, spaced f<sub>m</sub> apart, with amplitude A|J<sub>n</sub>(β)|. A negative J<sub>n</sub> is a 180° phase reversal. In theory the lines never end; in practice they die out quickly once n exceeds β.

Power. Each line carries (A J<sub>n</sub>)²/2 in 1 Ω, and Σ J<sub>n</sub>²(β) = 1, so the total is always A²/2. Modulation only moves power from the carrier to the sidebands. At β = 2.405, J<sub>0</sub> = 0 and the carrier disappears, all the power being in the sidebands; this null is used to calibrate deviation meters.

answer.text: Worked values. A = 10 V into 50 Ω (total 1 W), β = 2, f<sub>m</sub> = 5 kHz:

answer: Narrowband FM. For β ≤ about 0.2, J<sub>0</sub> ≈ 1, J<sub>1</sub> ≈ β/2 and J<sub>2</sub> is tiny (at β = 0.2: 0.9900, 0.0995, 0.0050). The wave is a carrier and one pair, bandwidth 2f<sub>m</sub>, like AM; but the lower sideband is negative, so the pair's resultant is at 90° to the carrier and the envelope hardly changes. An envelope detector cannot recover NBFM.

Wideband FM. For β of 1 or more several J<sub>n</sub> are large, and the carrier may be small or negative (J<sub>0</sub>(5) = −0.178). The bandwidth grows with the deviation; broadcast FM uses β = 5 for a 15 kHz tone.

answer.text: Carson's rule. Counting β + 1 significant pairs, each f<sub>m</sub> wide on both sides:

answer: Justification. For n > β + 1 the J<sub>n</sub> fall off fast, so the pairs beyond carry little power. In the table, the Carson band n ≤ 3 (30 kHz) holds 0.998 W of 1 W, 99.8 %; for β = 5 the 6 pairs hold 99.4 %. The two limits agree with the physics: for small β it gives 2f<sub>m</sub> (NBFM), for large β about 2Δf, the band the carrier sweeps.
Closing check. Broadcast FM, Δf = 75 kHz and W = 15 kHz: B<sub>T</sub> = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz, against 2Δf = 150 kHz; the extra 2f<sub>m</sub> = 30 kHz is the part the swept-band picture misses.

Direct FM drifts, so an AFC loop to a crystal reference is added
Indirect (Armstrong): integrator and narrowband phase modulator on a crystal oscillator give NBFM with a very small β
Multipliers raise carrier and deviation by the same factor N
A mixer between the multipliers shifts the carrier without changing the deviation
Compare stability, linearity and complexity

answer.text: Role of the varactor. A reverse-biased junction is a capacitor whose value falls as the reverse voltage rises. In the tank it sets

answer: Example. L = 1 µH and C = 25 pF give f<sub>0</sub> = 31.83 MHz. A ±0.5 pF swing gives +323.2 kHz and −313.6 kHz: about ±318 kHz, but unequal, which is the second-harmonic distortion of direct FM. A reactance modulator, a transistor made to look like a capacitor proportional to its g<sub>m</sub>, does the same job.

AFC. The LC centre frequency drifts with temperature and supply. The mixer and discriminator in the loop produce a slow dc voltage proportional to the frequency error, which is added to the varactor bias. The loop filter is slow, so it corrects drift but not the audio deviation.

Indirect (Armstrong) method, block diagram: audio → integrator → narrowband phase modulator driven by a crystal oscillator → multiplier N<sub>1</sub> → mixer with a crystal local oscillator → band-pass filter → multiplier N<sub>2</sub> → power amplifier (Figure 3.3.1).

Narrowband phase modulator. The crystal carrier is split; one path is shifted 90° and fed to a balanced modulator with the integrated audio; adding it back to the carrier gives A cos ω_c t − Aβ sin ω_m t sin ω_c t, the NBFM wave. It is linear only for small β, so the deviation is set to keep β ≤ 0.2 at the lowest audio frequency.

answer.text: Multipliers and mixer. A ×N stage multiplies the instantaneous frequency: carrier and deviation both scale by N. A mixer shifts every frequency by f<sub>LO</sub>, so the carrier moves and the deviation does not. Design with a 100 kHz crystal, 20 Hz deviation (β = 0.2 at 100 Hz), and a 96 MHz, 75 kHz target:

answer: Why the mixer sits between the multipliers. The deviation needs 75 000/20 = 3750 times; doing all of it on the 100 kHz carrier would give 375 MHz. Mixing down after the first multiplier lets the second multiplier finish the deviation and land on the channel.

bank.q: With a circuit diagram, explain the Foster-Seeley discriminator and its S-curve. How does a slope detector differ from it?
outline: Slope detector: a tank tuned off f<sub>c</sub> turns frequency into amplitude, then an envelope detector; simple, nonlinear, passes AM
Foster-Seeley: primary tuned to f<sub>c</sub>, centre-tapped secondary tuned to f<sub>c</sub>; Cc and an RF choke put e<sub>p</sub> at the centre tap
D1 sees e<sub>p</sub> + e<sub>s</sub>/2, D2 sees e<sub>p</sub> − e<sub>s</sub>/2; output V1 − V2 is an S-curve zero at f<sub>c</sub>
Linear over the middle of the S-curve only
Needs a limiter: amplitude changes cancel only at f<sub>c</sub>

answer.text: Circuit. The primary L1C1 and the centre-tapped secondary L2 are both tuned to f<sub>c</sub>. The coupling capacitor Cc and the RF choke L3 put the full primary voltage e<sub>p</sub> between the centre tap and the midpoint of the two loads. D1 and D2, each with an RC load, give V1 and V2; the output is taken across both loads.

answer: Secondary phase. A tuned secondary driven through mutual inductance is in quadrature with the primary at resonance. Off resonance, with x = 2Q(f − f<sub>c</sub>)/f<sub>c</sub>, the half-secondary voltage is e<sub>s</sub>/2 = j e<sub>p</sub> k/(1 + jx): its angle is 90° − arctan x, below 90° above f<sub>c</sub> and above 90° below f<sub>c</sub>.

Diode voltages. D1 sees the phasor sum e<sub>p</sub> + e<sub>s</sub>/2 and D2 sees e<sub>p</sub> − e<sub>s</sub>/2. Each diode with its load is an envelope detector, so V1 = |e<sub>p</sub> + e<sub>s</sub>/2|, V2 = |e<sub>p</sub> − e<sub>s</sub>/2| and v<sub>o</sub> = V1 − V2.

answer: S-curve. Plotted against frequency, v<sub>o</sub> is zero at f<sub>c</sub>, positive above, negative below, and odd about f<sub>c</sub>: an S. It is nearly straight over the middle (here to about ±150 kHz), peaks at ±328 kHz and falls again beyond, where the tuned circuits no longer respond. The usable deviation must stay inside the straight part.

Limiter. Both V1 and V2 scale with the input amplitude, so at f<sub>c</sub> an amplitude change cancels, but at any other frequency it changes V1 − V2. A limiter must therefore come first; the ratio detector, a variant with a large capacitor across the loads, gives some limiting by itself.

Slope detector, the difference. A single tank tuned to one side of f<sub>c</sub> turns frequency into amplitude on its flank, then a diode envelope detector reads it. It has one diode and no balance: the output is not zero at f<sub>c</sub>, the flank is straight only over a small part of f<sub>r</sub>/Q, and AM passes straight through. bank.q: Explain pre-emphasis and de-emphasis with circuit diagrams, frequency-response curves and typical time constants. Why does FM noise rise with frequency?
outline: Discriminator output noise power density rises as f², so the treble is noisiest
Pre-emphasis: an RC network at the transmitter boosts the highs above f<sub>1</sub> = 1/(2πτ)
De-emphasis: an RC low-pass at the receiver with the same τ restores a flat response
τ = 50 µs (3183 Hz) in most countries, 75 µs (2122 Hz) in the Americas
Improvement I = (W/f<sub>1</sub>)³/[3(W/f<sub>1</sub> − arctan(W/f<sub>1</sub>))]
answer: Why the noise rises. The discriminator output is proportional to the frequency offset. A noise component f hertz from the carrier produces a phase wobble whose rate of change, and so the output voltage, is proportional to f. The output noise power density is N<sub>0</sub>f²/A<sub>c</sub>²: a parabola in power, a triangle in amplitude.
Why that hurts. Programme energy is mostly at low and middle frequencies, so the treble has the weakest signal where the noise is strongest.

bank.q: Explain FM stereo multiplexing with block diagrams of the transmitter and the receiver. What is the role of the 19 kHz pilot?
outline: L and R are matrixed into L + R (0–15 kHz) and L − R
L − R modulates a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier (DSB-SC), 23–53 kHz
The composite is L + R, the DSB-SC difference and a 19 kHz pilot at 8–10 % of the modulation
The pilot is half the subcarrier so the receiver can double it with the right phase
Receiver: discriminator, L + R low-pass, 19 kHz pilot recovery and doubler, synchronous detector for L − R, matrix, de-emphasis
A mono set plays L + R: compatible

svg.aria: FM stereo transmitter and receiver block diagrams with matrix, 19 kilohertz pilot, doubler, balanced modulator, product detector and de-emphasis

answer: Transmitter. The pre-emphasised L and R go to a matrix that forms L + R and L − R. L + R stays at 0–15 kHz. L − R drives a balanced modulator with a 38 kHz carrier, which gives DSB-SC sidebands from 23 to 53 kHz with no 38 kHz line. The 38 kHz comes from doubling a 19 kHz oscillator, and a small part of that 19 kHz is added as the pilot. The sum of the three is the composite baseband, which frequency modulates the carrier with 75 kHz peak deviation.

answer.text: The composite spectrum (Figure 3.8.1):

head: part
band
content
rows: DSB-SC on a suppressed 38 kHz carrier

answer: Receiver. The discriminator gives back the composite. A 0–15 kHz low-pass gives L + R. A narrow 19 kHz filter or a phase-locked loop picks out the pilot; doubling gives 38 kHz locked in phase to the transmitter's subcarrier. A band-pass 23–53 kHz filter and a product detector with that 38 kHz recover L − R. The matrix forms L = [(L + R) + (L − R)]/2 and R = [(L + R) − (L − R)]/2, then de-emphasis acts on each output.

Role of the pilot. Coherent detection of DSB-SC needs a carrier of exactly the right frequency and phase. Because the transmitter's 38 kHz is the doubled 19 kHz, doubling the received pilot rebuilds it exactly. The pilot sits in the empty 15–23 kHz gap, costs little modulation, and lights the stereo indicator.

Phase accuracy. A phase error φ scales the detected L − R by cos φ, and the left output becomes L(1 + cos φ)/2 + R(1 − cos φ)/2. Separation = 20 log[(1 + cos φ)/(1 − cos φ)]: 42.3 dB at 10°, 22.9 dB at 30°.
Compatibility. A mono set filters at 15 kHz and plays L + R, the full programme. A stereo set on a mono station finds no pilot and plays L + R on both speakers.
Bandwidth. Carson with the 53 kHz baseband gives 2(75 + 53) = 256 kHz, against 180 kHz for mono.
Closing check with L = 1 V, R = 0.5 V: L + R = 1.5 V, L − R = 0.5 V; the matrix returns (1.5 + 0.5)/2 = 1.0 V and (1.5 − 0.5)/2 = 0.5 V.

answer: Modulation index β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> = 8/2 = 4. This is wideband FM (β well above 0.2).

Power. The envelope is constant at 10 V, so:
Spectrum. Lines at 10 MHz ± n × 2 kHz, amplitude 10|J<sub>n</sub>(4)| V, power (10 J<sub>n</sub>)²/100 for the carrier and twice that for a pair:

bank.q: An Armstrong transmitter starts with a crystal oscillator at 1 MHz and an NBFM modulator that gives a peak deviation of 200 Hz. Design the multiplier chain and the mixer needed to reach a carrier of 100 MHz with 75 kHz deviation.
outline: Total multiplication N = 75 000/200 = 375
Split it, N<sub>1</sub> = 15 and N<sub>2</sub> = 25, with a mixer between
After ×15: 15 MHz, 3 kHz; mix down to 100/25 = 4 MHz with an 11 MHz LO
After ×25: 100 MHz, 75 kHz
The mixer leaves the deviation unchanged; a single ×375 would give 375 MHz and need a 275 MHz LO
answer: Multipliers scale carrier and deviation together; a mixer shifts only the carrier. The deviation must grow from 200 Hz to 75 kHz, so the total multiplication is fixed by the deviation alone.

answer.text: Total multiplication:

answer: Single-chain option. ×375 on the 1 MHz carrier gives 375 MHz with 75 kHz deviation; a mixer with a 275 MHz local oscillator (difference) moves it to 100 MHz. It works on paper, but every stage after the multiplier runs at 375 MHz, and a 275 MHz crystal-derived LO is itself a chain.
Split-chain design. Put the mixer between two groups: N<sub>1</sub> × N<sub>2</sub> = 375. Choose N<sub>1</sub> = 15 (×3, ×5) and N<sub>2</sub> = 25 (×5, ×5).

answer.text: Stage by stage:

answer: Choosing the LO. The second group needs 100/25 = 4 MHz at its input, so f<sub>LO</sub> = 15 − 4 = 11 MHz (difference kept). f<sub>LO</sub> = 19 MHz, keeping 19 − 15 = 4 MHz, also works. A band-pass filter after the mixer passes 4 MHz and rejects the other product (26 MHz or 34 MHz).
Narrowband check. 200 Hz is small: with audio down to 1 kHz, β = 0.2 at the phase modulator, so the NBFM stage stays linear. At 15 kHz, β = 0.013 there and 75/15 = 5 at the output.

Stability. The LO should be crystal-controlled, since any LO error is multiplied by N<sub>2</sub> = 25 at the output (1 Hz error gives 25 Hz), and the 1 MHz crystal error is multiplied by 15 before the mixer and by 25 after it, 375 times in all.
Closing check: 1 MHz × 15 = 15 MHz; 15 − 11 = 4 MHz; 4 × 25 = 100 MHz; 200 Hz × 15 × 25 = 75 kHz.

Carrier plus narrowband noise; the quadrature noise sets the phase error n<sub>s</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>
Output noise density N<sub>0</sub>f²/A<sub>c</sub>²; power 2N<sub>0</sub>W³/(3A<sub>c</sub>²)
Signal Δf²/2; FOM = (3/2)β² (noise in W), or 3β²(β + 1) with noise in B<sub>T</sub>
AM: m²/(2 + m²), at most 1/3
Output SNR grows as β² for a fixed received power while the bandwidth grows as β
The trade stops at threshold, about 10 dB carrier-to-noise in B<sub>T</sub>
answer: Receiver model. A band-pass filter of width B<sub>T</sub> = 2(β + 1)W passes the FM wave and the noise; a limiter and an ideal discriminator follow, then a low-pass filter of width W. The channel noise is white with two-sided density N<sub>0</sub>/2. The received wave is A<sub>c</sub> cos[2πf<sub>c</sub> t + φ(t)] with φ(t) = β sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t, f<sub>m</sub> = W.

n(t) = n<sub>c</sub>(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub> t − n<sub>s</sub>(t) sin 2πf<sub>c</sub> t
n<sub>c</sub>, n<sub>s</sub>: low-pass, density N<sub>0</sub> each over |f| ≤ B<sub>T</sub>/2

Discriminator output. It gives (1/2π) dθ/dt:
answer.pre:
y(t) = (1/2π) dφ/dt + (1/2πA<sub>c</sub>) dn_s/dt
     = Δf cos 2πf<sub>m</sub> t + n<sub>d</sub>(t)

answer.text: Output noise. Differentiation multiplies the spectrum by (2πf)², so n<sub>d</sub> has density N<sub>0</sub>f²/A<sub>c</sub>² over |f| ≤ B<sub>T</sub>/2. The low-pass filter keeps |f| ≤ W:
answer.pre: N<sub>o</sub> = ∫ N<sub>0</sub> f²/A<sub>c</sub>² df, from −W to W, = 2N<sub>0</sub> W³/(3A<sub>c</sub>²)

answer.text: Output SNR and FOM:

answer: With the input noise measured in B<sub>T</sub> instead of W, the same result reads 3β²(β + 1).

answer.text: Comparison with AM (envelope detector, noise in W) and the coherent systems:

answer: The trade. For a fixed received power and noise, the output SNR grows as β² while the bandwidth grows roughly as β: doubling β from 5 to 10 adds 6.0 dB of output SNR for 22W/12W = 1.8 times the bandwidth. The reason is physical: the signal output grows with the deviation Δf, while the discriminator noise depends only on N<sub>0</sub>, A<sub>c</sub> and W, not on Δf.

The limit. The derivation assumed A<sub>c</sub> much larger than the noise in B<sub>T</sub>. As β grows, B<sub>T</sub> grows and so does the noise power N<sub>0</sub>B<sub>T</sub>. When the carrier-to-noise ratio ρ = (A<sub>c</sub>²/2)/(N<sub>0</sub>B<sub>T</sub>) falls to about 10 dB, the noise begins to swing the phasor round the origin, the output fills with clicks and the FOM collapses: the threshold. Since B<sub>T</sub> = 2(β + 1)W, threshold needs a channel SNR of about 20(β + 1): 120 (20.8 dB) for β = 5, 220 (23.4 dB) for β = 10.
So for a given received power there is a best β: the largest one that keeps the carrier above threshold. Threshold-extension receivers (FMFB, PLL) push this limit down by a few dB.
Closing check: β = 5, channel SNR 120: (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = 120 × 37.5 = 4500 = 36.5 dB, and ρ = 120/12 = 10 (10 dB) with 3β²(β + 1)ρ = 450 × 10 = 4500, the same value.

bank.q: Explain the threshold effect in FM. Define threshold and capture ratio, sketch the output SNR curve, and describe two methods of extending the threshold.
outline: Threshold: the carrier-to-noise ratio in B<sub>T</sub> at which the output SNR falls 1 dB below the straight-line law, about 10 dB
Cause: noise swings the resultant phasor round the origin, giving 2π phase jumps and clicks
Sketch: straight line above threshold, sharp knee, steep fall below
Capture ratio: the power ratio needed for the stronger of two co-channel signals to take over
Extension: FMFB narrows the IF bandwidth by feedback; a PLL detector tracks the phase with a narrow loop
Cost: complexity, loop stability, limited deviation range
answer: Above threshold. With ρ = C/(N<sub>0</sub>B<sub>T</sub>), the carrier-to-noise ratio in the IF bandwidth, the output follows (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = 3β²(β + 1)ρ: a straight line of slope 1 on a dB plot.

Cause of the threshold. The received phasor is the carrier plus a noise phasor. While the carrier is much longer, the noise only tilts it slightly. As ρ falls toward 10 dB, the noise phasor is now and then longer than the carrier and swings the resultant right round the origin. The phase jumps by 2π in a short time; the discriminator, which differentiates the phase, outputs a spike of area 1 cycle: a click. The click rate rises steeply as ρ falls, and clicks carry far more power than the smooth noise.

Definition. The threshold is the ρ at which the output SNR is 1 dB below the straight-line law; for usual tone-modulated receivers it is about 10 dB (some books use 13 dB, ρ = 20, as the onset of clicks). In channel-SNR terms it is about 20(β + 1).

answer.text: Numbers for the sketch (β = 5 and β = 2, W = 15 kHz, N<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz):

answer: Sketch (Figure 3.6.1). Output SNR against carrier power: each line rises 1 dB per dB above its threshold point, then falls steeply to the left of it. The β = 5 line is higher but starts 3 dB further right: wide deviation needs a stronger carrier.

Capture effect. With two FM signals on one channel, the limiter output follows the stronger, and the weaker only wobbles its phase slightly. The capture ratio is the smallest power ratio, in dB, of the stronger to the weaker at which the receiver follows the stronger cleanly; a few dB in good receivers. Example: −70 dBm against −75 dBm with a 3 dB capture ratio: 5 dB > 3 dB, so the −70 dBm station is heard. Capture lets FM reuse channels at shorter distances than AM, but a receiver can switch suddenly when the two levels cross.

Threshold extension 1, FM feedback (FMFB). The discriminator output drives the local oscillator so that it follows the incoming frequency. The IF signal then has a compressed deviation and can pass through a narrower filter, so less noise enters and the threshold falls. The loop must be stable and fast enough for the audio.

Threshold extension 2, phase-locked loop detector. A VCO is locked to the incoming wave; the loop control voltage is the demodulated audio. The loop bandwidth needs only cover the message, not B<sub>T</sub>, so it sees less noise and slips cycles (clicks) less often. A loop that is too narrow fails on large deviation.
Cost. Both trade circuit complexity and a limited deviation range for a few dB of threshold, which mattered most for weak links such as early satellite and space receivers.

bank.q: An FM broadcast service is to be planned for a city. Using deviation, Carson bandwidth, transmitter and detector choice, threshold, pre-emphasis and stereo multiplexing, justify the choice of each block in the transmitter and receiver chain and state which blocks decide the final audio quality.
outline: Deviation ±75 kHz, audio 15 kHz: β = 5; Carson 180 kHz mono, 256 kHz stereo
Transmitter: crystal-referenced exciter (PLL or Armstrong), pre-emphasis 50 µs, stereo coder
Receiver: RF stage, mixer to 10.7 MHz, IF filter, limiter, discriminator, stereo decoder, de-emphasis
Threshold sets the coverage edge; capture sets co-channel reuse
Quality is decided by deviation and emphasis, IF bandwidth and linearity, limiter, discriminator linearity, pilot phase
answer: Deviation and audio band. Choose the standard ±75 kHz peak deviation and W = 15 kHz: β = D = 5. With noise in the message band, FOM = (3/2) × 25 = 37.5 (15.7 dB) over plain baseband, and 20.5 dB over AM at m = 1.

answer.text: Bandwidth:
answer.pre:
mono:   B<sub>T</sub> = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz
stereo: B<sub>T</sub> = 2(75 + 53) = 256 kHz

answer: The stereo signal is wider than one 200 kHz channel, so stations in one city are placed several channels apart and the IF filter of the receiver is about 200 kHz wide, accepting a little loss of the outer sidebands.

Transmitter exciter. A crystal-referenced exciter is needed to hold the carrier within a few hundred hertz. Today this is a VCO in a phase-locked loop (direct FM with crystal stability); the Armstrong chain (for example 100 kHz, 20 Hz, ×75, mixer, ×50 to 96 MHz with 75 kHz) does the same by multiplication. Direct FM without AFC is ruled out by drift.

Pre-emphasis. 50 µs (corner 3183 Hz) as used in most countries; the receivers sold in the city must match it. It improves the output SNR by 10.4 (10.2 dB) for a 15 kHz band, at the cost of a higher peak deviation on bright music, so an audio limiter after the pre-emphasis keeps the peak at 75 kHz.

Stereo coder. L + R at 0–15 kHz for mono listeners, a 19 kHz pilot at about 9 % of the modulation, L − R on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier, all within the 75 kHz peak. Optionally RDS at 57 kHz for the station name.

Receiver. RF amplifier for noise figure and image rejection; mixer to 10.7 MHz, which puts the image 21.4 MHz away, outside the 20 MHz band; ceramic IF filter about 200 kHz wide for adjacent-channel selectivity; limiter to remove AM; discriminator (ratio, quadrature or digital) with a straight S-curve over ±75 kHz plus margin; stereo decoder with PLL pilot recovery; de-emphasis on L and R; audio amplifiers.

answer.text: Coverage. With N<sub>0</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz and B<sub>T</sub> = 180 kHz, the noise is −121.4 dBm and the threshold carrier −111.4 dBm for an ideal receiver. A receiver with noise figure F raises both by F dB. Inside the coverage the target output SNR, say 50 dB for good stereo, sets the needed carrier:

answer: Stereo costs SNR: the L − R channel is noisier than L + R because the 23–53 kHz band sits higher on the noise parabola, so the stereo service area is smaller than the mono one; receivers blend to mono on weak signals.

Co-channel and adjacent planning. Capture lets a co-channel station be reused once its signal is a capture ratio (a few dB) below the wanted one everywhere in the service area; adjacent channels are kept away by the IF selectivity and by spacing.

answer.text: Which blocks decide quality:

head: block
effect
rows: too narrow or uneven gives distortion and poor separation

answer: Evaluation. More deviation would raise the SNR (as β²) but widen the signal and raise the threshold power; less would save spectrum but cost SNR. ±75 kHz with 50 µs emphasis is the accepted balance for city broadcasting with cheap receivers.
Closing check: 2(75 + 53) = 256 kHz; −111.4 dBm − (−121.4 dBm) = 10 dB at threshold; 10 + 26.5 = 36.5 dB output there.

The rate at which the carrier phase advances, f<sub>i</sub> = (1/2π) dθ/dt, in hertz.
The largest amount by which the instantaneous frequency moves away from f<sub>c</sub>, in hertz.
Δf/f<sub>m</sub> for a tone; it sets how many sideband pairs carry significant power.
FM with β up to about 0.2, whose spectrum is a carrier and one sideband pair in 2f<sub>m</sub>.
FM with β of order 1 or more, whose spectrum spreads over many sideband pairs.

J<sub>n</sub>(β), the amplitude factor of the n-th sideband of a tone-modulated FM wave.
A reverse-biased diode used as a voltage-controlled capacitor in direct FM oscillators.
A nonlinear stage tuned to the N-th harmonic; it multiplies carrier and deviation by N.
Indirect FM: integrate the audio, make NBFM from a crystal with a phase modulator, then multiply and mix.

A circuit whose output voltage is proportional to the frequency offset from f<sub>c</sub>.

An IF stage that clips the FM wave to a constant amplitude before the discriminator.
Output SNR over channel SNR, used to compare modulation schemes for the same received power and noise.
The sharp fall of FM output SNR, with clicks, once the carrier-to-noise ratio in the IF band drops to about 10 dB.
A spike at the discriminator output when noise swings the resultant phasor round the origin.
The power ratio in dB by which a co-channel FM signal must exceed another to take over the receiver.
A treble boost of time constant τ at the FM transmitter, before the modulator.
The matching treble cut after the discriminator; it restores flat audio and cuts the treble noise.
The 19 kHz tone in FM stereo that the receiver doubles to rebuild the 38 kHz subcarrier.
The FM stereo modulating signal: L + R, the pilot, and L − R on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier.
